extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of philosophy (ethics/Aristotle)
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and study of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics (Book I), focusing on definitions and method for identifying the Chief Good (Happiness) and the proper approach to moral philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every art aims at some good / Chief Good as ultimate end
rubrics_metrics.description: “Every art, and every science reduced to a teachable form, and in like manner every action and moral choice, aims ... at some good: for which reason a common ... description of the Chief Good is, ‘that which all things aim at.’”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the teleological framework: when analysing any action, art, or science, identify its end (the good it aims at). To locate the Chief Good for human life, find the end which other ends are pursued for. Examples given: healing→health, ship-building→a vessel, military art→victory. Implication: treat ethical inquiry as the search for the ultimate end that gives intelligibility to other ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finality (absolutely final) as criterion for the Chief Good
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chief Good must be ‘absolutely final’ — an object of choice always in itself and never chosen with a view to something else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate candidate goods by whether they are chosen for their own sake only (happiness is argued to have this property), as opposed to honour, pleasure, or wealth, which are also chosen as means to something else. Use the test: would one choose X for X alone, or always with some ulterior aim?

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-sufficiency as a mark of the final good
rubrics_metrics.description: The final good should be self-sufficient: ‘which taken alone makes life choice-worthy, and to be in want of nothing;’ this is part of what qualifies Happiness as the Chief Good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a proposed highest good makes life complete/choice-worthy by itself (including appropriate social relations — family, friends, polis). Beware extending the scope indefinitely; the text notes a practical limit must be fixed when applying self-sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy of ends: prioritize master-arts' ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Ends of the master-arts are more choice-worthy than those ranging under them, because master-arts are pursued with a view to their ends and command other practical sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging aims or projects, place higher weight on more inclusive/master ends (e.g., polity/political science governs other practical sciences). Practical implication: in ethical or literary analysis, consider higher-level aims that make subordinate aims intelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish independent (intrinsic) goods from instrumental goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate independent goods (pursued for their own sakes — e.g., wisdom, certain pleasures, honours) from instrumental goods (pursued because they produce or preserve other goods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating values or motives, explicitly classify goods as intrinsic vs. instrumental. The text recommends examining whether an alleged good is chosen in itself or because it conduces to something else.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match level of exactness and method to subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Exactness must not be looked for in all discussions alike’ — different subjects admit different degrees of precision; it is absurd to demand demonstrative mathematical proof of rhetoric, or persuasion instead of proof in mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set appropriate standards of rigour for the domain studied: expect demonstrative proof where applicable, but accept general, rough, outline conclusions in areas (like ethics/political thought) where data and variability preclude strict exactness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience and disposition required for moral inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The young man is not a fit student of Moral Philosophy, for he has no experience in the actions of life and is prone to follow his passions; moral study presupposes habits and some life-experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate readiness of students/readers by their experiential background and self-control. Moral theorising is fruitful only for those whose dispositions allow them to receive and apply principles; youthful impulsiveness or lack of formed habits make study unprofitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the human function: rational activity as criterion of human good
rubrics_metrics.description: To discover the Good of man, determine man’s proper work: not mere life or sensation (shared with plants/animals) but the life of the Rational Nature apt to act — i.e., rational activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a function/ergon argument: identify what is peculiar to the thing evaluated (here, humans) and base the account of excellence/good on fulfilling that function well. For humans, assess the quality of rational activity to judge human flourishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical thought in conduct should reveal situation (situated reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The thinking which really matters in conduct is ... thinking which reveals to the agent the situation ... both the universal situation ... and the ever-varying ... situation in which he as this individual, here and now, finds himself.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appraising moral action or practical decision-making, prioritize contextual, situational judgement over mere instrumental calculation or idealized forecasting. Good practical reasoning attends both to general principles and the particulars of the present case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject equating happiness with honour/pleasure/wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Honour, pleasure, and wealth are argued not to be adequate accounts of the Chief Good: honour depends on others, pleasure is slavish and brute, wealth is instrumental, and each can be insufficient as a complete life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating candidate conceptions of the good, test them for independence, self-sufficiency, and stability. Beware superficial accounts that make the highest good depend on external validation or merely on pleasurable states.
